title: A Second Warning
sum: Twenty years into his reign, with the temple and palace finished, Solomon hears from God a second time. The promise of Gibeon is now a warning. If Solomon and his sons keep the LORD's rules, David's throne will stand; if they turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land and the temple will become a byword, a ruin people whistle at in shock.

The rest of the chapter is a ledger of Solomon's power: towns handed to Hiram of Tyre in payment, which Hiram calls worthless; a forced-labor system that builds Jerusalem's wall and the fortified cities of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer; a pharaoh's daughter with a city as her dowry; and a Red Sea fleet bringing gold from Ophir. The reader who has just heard the warning is left to wonder what all this building will be worth.
readings: Read as a hinge

Chapters 1–8 rise to the dedication of the temple; chapters 9–11 descend to Solomon's fall. God's speech in 9:1–9 stands at the turning point. It repeats the conditions of 2:4 and 8:25, and everything that follows can be read in its light: wealth, wives and horses are the very things Deuteronomy 17 warned a king against.
Read as royal annals

Much of the chapter reads like a list from court records: payments, building projects, labor policy, trade. Historians mine it for the administration of an early state. Its lists are uneven, and the Greek translation puts several of them in other places, which suggests that editors arranged the material from older notes.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as a record of Solomon's middle years, about 950 BC. The building at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, the treaty with Tyre and the Ophir trade fit a strong king with access to the Red Sea, and the forced-labor notes are frank about the cost.
views.C: Critical scholars hear in 9:6–9 the voice of the exile: a temple already destroyed and a people scattered, explained as the result of idolatry. Many think the lists of 9:15–28 come from old administrative notes, but they debate how much is 10th-century and how much was written into Solomon's reign later.
views.A: This is the classic chapter for the 'Solomonic gates' debate (9:15). Six-chambered gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer were dated by Yigael Yadin to Solomon; many now date them to the 9th century. The Tell Qasile ostracon ('gold of Ophir') confirms Ophir as a trade name, and the Gezer note fits a period when Egypt meddled in Philistine and Canaanite cities.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads God's warning as one of the sources of the belief that the first temple was destroyed for idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed (Yoma 9b). The rabbis read the conditions of 9:4–9 as binding on every generation, which is why the fast of Tisha b'Av mourns the temple's fall as the result of Israel's sins rather than of Babylon's strength.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 9:7–9 the background to Jesus' warning about the second temple: 'not one stone will be left on another' (Matthew 24:2), and to his claim to be the true temple (John 2:19–21). The condition on David's throne points them to a son of David whose obedience did not fail.

deep.b:
Kings gives two pictures of Solomon's workforce. In 5:13–18 he drafts thirty thousand men "from all Israel" to work in Lebanon in shifts of a month on and two months off, besides seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters. In 9:20–22 the permanent slave labor falls only on the surviving Canaanite peoples, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers.

Some readers find a contradiction; others see two different systems, a temporary draft and a permanent slave force. Either way, the burden was real. Adoniram (Adoram) was in charge of it (4:6; 5:14), and when the northern tribes revolted after Solomon's death, the first thing they did was stone him (12:18). Jeroboam, the future king of the north, rose as a foreman of the Ephraimite labor gangs (11:28). The labor system is the thread that ties Solomon's glory to the kingdom's breakup.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the speech as a key to the ledger
deep.b: The chapter places God's warning (9:1–9) directly before a list of payments, labor and trade (9:10–28), with no comment between them. My suggestion is that the arrangement is deliberate and the list is meant to be read through the warning: Hiram's disappointment with the towns (9:12–13), the forced labor (9:15, 21) and the gold (9:28) are each things a reader of Deuteronomy would watch for. This overlaps with what Jerome Walsh, Iain Provan and others say about chapters 10–11, which they read as a quiet case against Solomon; I would start that case one chapter earlier.

echoes: 3:4–15; 8:22–53; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; Deuteronomy 28:37; Deuteronomy 29:24–26; Jeremiah 22:8–9; 2 Chronicles 7:11–22; 2 Chronicles 8:1–18; Matthew 24:1–2

settings.what: The LORD's second appearance to Solomon
settings.when: after the temple and palace are finished, about twenty years into his reign
settings.why: God says he has heard the prayer and made the house holy. Then he sets two roads before Solomon and his sons. If they walk as David did, the throne will stand. If they serve other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land, and the temple will become a ruin that makes passersby ask why. The answer is given in advance: they left the LORD. For readers who had seen the ruined temple, this was the book's explanation of their own history.
views: Traditional readers take it as God's word to Solomon, which his later sins made a sentence.
Many critical scholars see the description of the ruined house as written by the historian with the destruction of Jerusalem already in view.

title: The Queen of Sheba
sum: A queen from Sheba in southern Arabia comes to Jerusalem with a camel train of spices, gold and jewels to test Solomon with riddles. He answers every one. She sees his palace, his table, his servants and his worship, and it leaves her breathless. She praises the LORD who made Solomon king to do justice, and the two exchange royal gifts.

The chapter then tallies Solomon's wealth: 666 talents of gold a year, gold shields, an ivory throne with twelve lions, cups of gold, ships that return every three years with exotic cargo, fourteen hundred chariots, and horses bought from Egypt and Que. Silver is as common as stones. It is the height of Solomon's glory, and readers of Deuteronomy 17 will notice that it is also a list of what a king was told not to collect.
readings: Read as praise

On its surface the chapter celebrates Solomon. The queen's visit fulfills his prayer that foreigners would come to Jerusalem for the LORD's name (8:41–43), and her blessing names the true purpose of kingship: justice and right (10:9). The wealth is the blessing God promised in 3:13.
Read as warning

A closer reading sees the narrator setting up the fall of chapter 11. Gold, silver, horses from Egypt and, next, many wives are exactly the four things Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbids a king to multiply. The number 666 and the lion throne show a king at the summit, about to be judged by the standard he forgot.
Read through later traditions

The queen became a figure of legend in Ethiopia, Judaism and Islam. In Ethiopia she is Makeda, mother of Menelik and of a royal line; in the Qur'an she is the queen of Saba who submits to God with Solomon; in some Jewish legends she is a riddle-setter and even a demon. None of these details is in Kings, but they show how much readers have found in eleven verses.

views.H: Traditional readers take the visit as a real trade embassy and royal visit, about 950 BC. Southern Arabia controlled the incense trade, and a mission to the king who controlled the roads north and the Red Sea ports makes good commercial sense.
views.C: Critical scholars note that Sabaean records are thin before about 800 BC and that Arabian queens appear in Assyrian texts only in the 8th century. Many read the story as a legend shaped by later trade and by Psalm 72's picture of kings bringing gifts, written to glorify Solomon's wisdom.
views.A: Camel caravans, frankincense, gold of Ophir and ivory are all attested in the first millennium BC. The Sabaean kingdom's capital at Marib and its temple are known from excavations. Lion thrones and ivory furniture are known from Megiddo and Samaria. No outside source mentions Solomon or the queen.
views.J: The rabbis debated the queen. One view in the Talmud reads 'malkat Sheva' as 'the kingdom of Sheba' and denies she was a woman at all (Bava Batra 15b). The Targum Sheni to Esther tells how a hoopoe carried Solomon's letter to her and gives her riddles. Medieval legend made her a seductress or demoness, linked with Lilith.
views.X: Jesus said 'the queen of the south' would rise at the judgment and condemn his generation, 'for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look, something greater than Solomon is here' (Matthew 12:42, fresh rendering). Church fathers read her as a figure of the Gentile church coming to Christ, and connected her gifts with the Magi's.

deep.b:
Ethiopia. The Kebra Nagast, compiled in the 14th century from older traditions, calls her Makeda, queen of Ethiopia. She visits Solomon, converts to the God of Israel, and bears his son Menelik, who later carries the ark of the covenant to Aksum. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church still claims to hold the ark, and Ethiopia's emperors traced their line to Menelik until 1974. Ethiopia's Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jews) and its Christian church both tell versions of the story.

Islam. Qur'an 27:20–44 tells how a hoopoe brings Solomon (Sulayman) news of a queen of Saba whose people worship the sun. Solomon writes to her, her throne is brought to him in a moment, and she enters a palace with a floor of glass, mistakes it for water, and lifts her skirts. She then submits "with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds." Later Muslim writers name her Bilqis.

Judaism. The Targum Sheni to Esther has the hoopoe story and the riddles. Some rabbis denied she was a queen at all (Bava Batra 15b). Medieval legend, collected by Jacob Lassner, made her hairy-legged, a demon or a seductress, partly from discomfort with a powerful foreign woman.

The historical debate. Some historians accept a 10th-century Arabian trade mission; others think the story was told back into Solomon's reign from later Arabian contacts. The text itself is interested in her as a witness: a wise foreigner who comes, tests and blesses Israel's God.

echoes: 3:12–13; 4:29–34; 8:41–43; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Psalm 72:10–15; Isaiah 60:6; Matthew 2:11; Matthew 6:29; Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31; Luke 12:27; Revelation 13:18; 2 Chronicles 9:1–28

settings.when: after she has tested him with hard questions and seen his court and his offerings
settings.why: The queen says the reports did not tell her half, calls his servants fortunate, and blesses the LORD, who made Solomon king "to do what is just and right." A foreign ruler names the purpose of kingship. Her praise marks the height of Solomon's glory. Readers who know chapter 11 hear it also as a reminder of what he would lose. Jesus pointed to her in Matthew 12:42.

title: The Torn Kingdom
sum: Solomon loves many foreign women, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and in his old age they bend his heart to other gods. He builds high places for Chemosh and Molech facing Jerusalem. The LORD, who appeared to him twice, announces that he will tear the kingdom away, not in Solomon's lifetime and not all of it: one tribe will stay with David's line for David's sake and Jerusalem's.

God raises opponents: Hadad of Edom, sheltered in Egypt; Rezon, who takes Damascus; and Jeroboam son of Nebat, one of Solomon's own labor foremen. The prophet Ahijah meets Jeroboam on the road, tears a new cloak into twelve pieces, and gives him ten. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Shishak of Egypt. After forty years Solomon dies and his son Rehoboam takes the throne.
readings: Read as judgment

The narrator's verdict is moral and theological. Solomon broke the first commandment, and the kingdom is torn as Saul's was. Every disaster in the chapter is traced to the LORD: he raises the opponents, he tears the kingdom, he chooses Jeroboam.
Read as politics

Historians read the same events as the unraveling of an overextended state. Edom and Damascus break free on the edges, a capable official builds a following among the overworked northern tribes, and Egypt's new dynasty shelters the rebels. The narrator does not deny any of this; he explains why it happened.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as the last decade of Solomon's reign, about 940–931 BC, with Solomon's apostasy as a real turn in old age. Christian and Jewish tradition debated whether he repented, often reading Ecclesiastes as his late confession.
views.C: Most critical scholars see the hand of the Deuteronomistic editor in 11:1–13 and 11:31–39, judging Solomon by Deuteronomy's laws on marriage and worship. The opponents of 11:14–25 are often thought to come from older records; some think they troubled Solomon from the start of his reign and were placed here to show judgment.
views.A: Edom's rise as a state and Damascus's growth in the 10th–9th centuries are attested archaeologically and in Assyrian records. Shishak (Shoshenq I) is a known pharaoh whose reign began about 945 BC, which fits Jeroboam's flight late in Solomon's reign.
views.J: The Talmud preserves both a defense ('Whoever says Solomon sinned is mistaken,' Shabbat 56b) and a lesson: the Torah gave reasons for its laws on wives and horses, and Solomon thought he could keep the reason without the rule, and fell (Sanhedrin 21b). Midrash also says that on the day Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, the angel Gabriel planted a reed in the sea that grew into Rome (Shabbat 56b).
views.X: Nehemiah 13:26 made Solomon a warning about mixed marriages. Christian writers took him as the great example of a wise man brought down, and debated his salvation; Cyril of Jerusalem counted him among the penitent (Catecheses 2.13). Ben Sira had already judged that Solomon gave his body to women and so brought wrath on his children and split the kingdom (Sirach 47:19–21). The promise of 'a lamp' for David (11:36) and 'not for all time' (11:39) are read as a hope that points to Christ, the son of David.

deep.h: Solomon's apostasy: how readers have judged it
deep.b:
A real fall. Most readers take the text at its word: Solomon worshiped other gods in his old age. The narrator says it plainly, and the punishment is the loss of most of the kingdom. Many Christian preachers have used Solomon as a warning that wisdom, wealth and religious achievement do not protect a person from gradual drift.

A fault of toleration. One rabbinic view says Solomon did not personally worship idols but failed to stop his wives, and Scripture counts it against him as if he had (Shabbat 56b). Some Christian interpreters held similar views.

Repentance. Jewish tradition says Solomon wrote the Song of Songs in youth, Proverbs in middle age and Ecclesiastes in old age (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:10), and many readers find in Ecclesiastes a man who has tried everything and returned to fearing God. Kings says nothing of repentance.

Political marriages. Historians stress that diplomatic marriages required giving foreign wives their own chapels, as Solomon did (11:8). What a modern state would call religious freedom for foreign envoys, Deuteronomy calls apostasy.

echoes: 3:1; 9:4–9; Exodus 34:15–16; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Deuteronomy 17:17; Joshua 23:12–13; 1 Samuel 15:27–28; 2 Samuel 7:14–16; 2 Kings 23:13; Nehemiah 13:26; Ecclesiastes 2:1–11; Sirach 47:19–21

settings.what: The law against marrying the nations
settings.by: the narrator, quoting the LORD's command through Moses
settings.to: the Israelites, and here King Solomon
settings.when: when Solomon loves many foreign women
settings.why: The narrator cites the law that Israel must not marry the peoples of the land, because they will turn Israel's hearts to their gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4; compare Exodus 34:16). It bound every Israelite, and the law of the king added that he must not take many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). The law answered the danger of idolatry through marriage. Solomon's seven hundred wives show the danger come true, and readers who returned from exile faced the same question (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:26).

settings.when: when Solomon, old, builds high places for the gods of his wives
settings.why: God says he will tear the kingdom away and give it to Solomon's servant. But he will not do it in Solomon's lifetime, for David's sake, and he will not take all of it: one tribe will stay, for David and for Jerusalem. The sentence explains to readers both why the kingdom split and why Judah survived it.

settings.by: Ahijah the prophet from Shiloh, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Jeroboam son of Nebat, Solomon's overseer of forced labor from the tribes of Joseph, alone with him in the open country
settings.why: Ahijah tears his new cloak into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten, as a sign that God will give him ten tribes. He names Solomon's worship of other gods as the reason. God keeps one tribe for David's line "so that a lamp will burn for David," and offers Jeroboam a lasting house like David's if he obeys. The oracle makes the split God's own act, not just a revolt. It also sets the test Jeroboam will fail. The torn cloak recalls Samuel's torn robe (1 Samuel 15:27–28), and the word "though not for all time" (11:39) gave later readers hope for David's line.
views: Ahijah came from Shiloh, the old sanctuary of the northern tribes, and many scholars think his words first circulated in the north, where the split was seen as God's justice.
Gerhard von Rad showed how Kings is built on prophecies and their fulfillments, and this oracle begins a chain that runs through the whole book (12:15; 15:29).

title: Rehoboam's Answer
sum: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king by the northern tribes, who ask him to lighten the heavy yoke his father laid on them. The elders advise him to serve the people for a day and win them forever; his boyhood friends tell him to threaten whips and scorpions. He takes the young men's advice. Israel answers with the old cry of rebellion, stones the labor chief, and makes Jeroboam king. Only Judah, with Benjamin, stays with David's house, and a prophet forbids civil war.

Jeroboam fortifies Shechem and fears that pilgrimage to Jerusalem will draw his people back. So he makes two gold calves, sets them at Bethel and Dan with the words of Aaron at Sinai, appoints non-Levite priests, and moves the autumn festival a month later. The narrator calls it simply 'sin.'
readings: Read as God's judgment
The narrator says the split was 'a turn from the LORD' to fulfill Ahijah's word (12:15) and 'from me' (12:24). Solomon's idolatry is the root cause.
Read as a study in leadership

The scene of the two councils is one of the Bible's sharpest portraits of power. The elders offer a paradox, serve to be served; the young men offer bravado. Rehoboam's choice shows a man who mistakes harshness for strength.
Read as tribal history

The north and the south had been joined only under David and Solomon. Shechem, Sheba's old slogan, and the labor chief's death show an old rivalry breaking out. Historians often see the split as a return to two peoples rather than the breaking of one.

views.H: Traditional readers date the split to 931/930 BC (Thiele, Galil, Kitchen); others give about 928 (Tadmor, Cogan), about 927/926 (Hayes and Hooker) or, in Albright's older system, 922. They take Jeroboam's shrines as a political move to keep his people from Jerusalem, the 'sin' that defined the north to its end in 722 BC.
views.C: Critical scholars see a southern, Jerusalem-centered writer judging the northern shrines by Deuteronomy's demand for one place of worship. Many think Bethel and Dan were old sanctuaries of the LORD and that the calves were pedestals, not idols. Some, such as Israel Finkelstein, doubt there was ever a strong united kingdom to divide.
views.A: At Tel Dan, Avraham Biran found a large cult platform and sacred precinct whose first phase he dated to Jeroboam's time. Bull figurines are known from Israelite sites, including the 'Bull Site' near Dothan. Penuel, Mahanaim and Succoth, east of the Jordan, appear in Shishak's campaign list at Karnak.
views.J: The Mishnah names Jeroboam first among the kings who 'have no share in the world to come' (Sanhedrin 10:2), and the Talmud has God offer to walk with him in Eden if he repents, but Jeroboam asks, 'Who will be first?' and refuses when told David will lead (Sanhedrin 102a). The rabbis saw his sin as political religion: worship arranged to protect a throne.
views.X: Christian readers have used Rehoboam's choice to illustrate Jesus' teaching that the greatest must be the servant (Mark 10:42–45). The calves are read with Exodus 32 and Acts 7:41 as the repeated pattern of making God in a manageable image, and the split as a wound that the prophets hoped would be healed under one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:22–24).

deep.h: The Greek's other story of Jeroboam (12:24a–z)
deep.b:
After 12:24 the Greek Septuagint, in Codex Vaticanus and most other manuscripts, adds a long passage that tells Jeroboam's rise a second time. In outline:

Jeroboam is the son of Sarira, a prostitute. Solomon puts him over the labor of the house of Joseph; he builds a fortress, gathers three hundred chariots and plots to take the kingdom. He flees to Shishak, who gives him Ano, the elder sister of his queen, as wife; she bears him a son, Abijah. When he returns to his land, his son falls sick, and Ano goes to the prophet Ahijah, who foretells the boy's death and the end of Jeroboam's house. Then at Shechem the prophet Shemaiah tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten. The meeting with Rehoboam follows, told again more briefly.

The Hebrew places these events in a different order (11:26–40; 12:1–20; 14:1–18) and lacks the details about Ano and the chariots. Some scholars, such as Adrian Schenker, argue that the Greek supplement preserves an older form of the story, from a Hebrew text that differed from the Masoretic one. Others, especially D. W. Gooding and Zipora Talshir, think it is a later Jewish retelling, a kind of midrash, assembled from the Hebrew chapters with some added color. Either way, it is a reminder that in Kings the Greek translation sometimes reflects a different edition, not just a different wording.

A note on the Greek witness: chapters 9–16 lie outside the so-called kaige section of the Greek Kings (a later revision toward the Hebrew, which in 1 Kings begins at chapter 22), so Codex Vaticanus and Rahlfs' edition are a good witness here to the Old Greek translation. The Greek variants given for these chapters rest on that text.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the baby who was not divided
deep.b: Solomon's reign opened with his most famous judgment: two women and one baby, and a king's order to cut the living child in two (3:16–28). The true mother would rather give the child away than see it divided; the false one says, "He won't be mine or yours. Cut!" (3:26). My suggestion is that chapter 12 is meant to recall that scene. Solomon's son is offered a choice between giving something up (lightening the yoke) and keeping everything, and by refusing to give up anything he gets a kingdom cut in two. He acts like the woman who would rather divide than yield. The verbs differ (gazar "cut" in chapter 3, qara' "tear" in chapter 11), so the link is thematic, not verbal. I have not seen this argued in detail, though literary readers often note how the wisdom of chapter 3 drains away by chapters 11–12.

echoes: 1 Samuel 8:11–18; 2 Samuel 5:1–3; 2 Samuel 20:1; Exodus 32:1–8; Judges 18:30; Genesis 28:10–22; Leviticus 23:33–43; Hosea 8:4–6; Mark 10:42–45; Acts 7:41; 2 Chronicles 10:1–11:17

settings.by: Jeroboam and the whole assembly of Israel
settings.to: Rehoboam son of Solomon, who has come to Shechem to be made king
settings.why: The tribes say Solomon made their yoke heavy and promise to serve Rehoboam if he lightens it. They are asking for the covenant between king and people to be renewed on fairer terms (compare 2 Samuel 5:3). Readers remember Samuel's warning (1 Samuel 8:11–18) and Solomon's labor draft (5:13–18).

settings.by: the elders who served Solomon, then the young men who grew up with Rehoboam
settings.when: during the three days he asks to think it over
settings.why: The elders say that if the king will be a servant to the people today, they will be his servants forever. The young men tell him to boast that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist and that he will punish with scorpions. The two speeches set out two views of power. Readers who heard Deuteronomy's law of the king, that he must not lift himself above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:20), knew which was right.

settings.to: Jeroboam and all the people, on the third day
settings.why: Rehoboam repeats the young men's threat word for word. The narrator adds that the LORD brought this about to fulfill Ahijah's word. The king's folly and God's plan work together. The speech costs David's house ten tribes.

settings.to: King Rehoboam and the house of David
settings.when: when the king refuses to listen
settings.why: The tribes answer with Sheba's old cry (2 Samuel 20:1): no share in David, to your tents, Israel. The words break the covenant made at Hebron (2 Samuel 5:1–3). The narrator says the split remains "to this day," so the first readers still lived with its results.

settings.by: Shemaiah, the man of God, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and the rest of the people
settings.when: as Rehoboam musters 180,000 men to win back the north
settings.why: God forbids them to fight their kinsmen, "because this thing has come from me." They obey and go home. The word tells readers in Judah that the split was God's judgment, to be accepted, not undone by war.

settings.what: Jeroboam's calves and his new feast
settings.to: the people of the northern tribes, at Bethel and Dan
settings.when: early in his reign, when he fears that pilgrims to Jerusalem will turn back to Rehoboam
settings.why: Jeroboam sets up two golden calves and tells the people, "Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt." He builds shrines on high places, appoints priests who are not Levites, and moves the autumn feast to the eighth month. These royal decrees bound the worship of the whole northern kingdom. They answered a political problem, but the narrator calls them sin, and "the sin of Jeroboam" becomes the charge against every northern king. His words repeat Aaron's at the golden calf (Exodus 32:4).
views: Many scholars think the calves were meant as pedestals for the invisible LORD, like the cherubim on the ark. On this view Jeroboam saw his worship as true worship of Israel's God at old holy places.

For Kings, any worship outside Jerusalem broke Deuteronomy 12's law of one chosen place, so whatever Jeroboam meant, it led Israel away. Readers in Judah, especially under Josiah, who tore down Bethel's altar (2 Kings 23:15), read the story this way.

title: The Man of God from Judah
sum: As Jeroboam stands at his new altar in Bethel, a man of God from Judah cries out against it: a son of David named Josiah will one day burn the bones of its priests on it. The altar splits, and the king's hand, stretched out to seize the prophet, goes stiff until the prophet prays. The man of God refuses the king's hospitality, as the LORD commanded him: no bread, no water, no return by the same road.

Then an old prophet of Bethel rides after him, claims an angel has told him otherwise, and brings him home to eat. At the table the liar receives a true word: the man of God will not be buried with his ancestors. On the road a lion kills him and stands guard over the body beside his donkey. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb and asks to be laid beside him, for the word against Bethel will surely come true. Jeroboam does not turn back.
readings: Read as a story about the word of God

The phrase 'by the LORD's word' runs through the chapter. A word spoken by the LORD is sure to happen (13:32) and must be obeyed even against a later, smoother voice. Both prophets learn this, one by dying and one by burying him.
Read as a parable of the two kingdoms

Karl Barth read the man of God and the old prophet as Judah and Israel: the faithful one deceived, the unfaithful one used to speak the truth, and both finally lying in one grave, which Josiah spares (2 Kings 23:18). The reading is theological, but the story invites it.
Read as a warning to prophets

The chapter tests prophecy itself. The man of God resists a king's bribe but falls for a colleague's lie. Deuteronomy's tests for prophets (Deuteronomy 13; 18) stand behind it: a word that contradicts the LORD's clear command is false, whoever speaks it.

views.H: Traditional readers take the story as an event at Bethel early in Jeroboam's reign, and the naming of Josiah as true prediction, fulfilled about 300 years later (2 Kings 23:15–18).
views.C: Most critical scholars think the story reached its present form in Josiah's time or later, to justify his destruction of the Bethel altar. Many see an older northern prophetic legend underneath, with the name Josiah added. The chapter interrupts the account of Jeroboam's reign (12:33 and 13:33 frame it).
views.A: Bethel's 10th–9th-century remains are poorly preserved, so the altar itself has not been found. The Tel Dan altar platform gives a picture of what Jeroboam's other shrine looked like. Lions survived in the land into the Middle Ages.
views.J: Josephus names the man of God Jadon and has the old prophet later explain away the signs to Jeroboam (Antiquities 8.230–245). The Talmud discusses the story under the law of the false prophet (Sanhedrin 89a–b) and remarks that a shared meal brought a true word even to a deceiver (Sanhedrin 103b). Some rabbinic sources identify the man of God with Iddo the seer (2 Chronicles 9:29).
views.X: Christian readers link the deceiving 'angel' with Paul's warning against any gospel, even from an angel, that contradicts the one received (Galatians 1:8), and the faithful prophet's failure with the call to persevere. Barth's reading of the two prophets as elect and rejected, joined in one grave, has been influential in modern theology.

deep.h: How 1 Kings 13 ends: Josiah at Bethel
deep.b:
Three centuries later King Josiah tore down Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, took bones from the tombs on the hillside and burned them on it, "just as the LORD's word had said, the word that the man of God called out" (2 Kings 23:16). Seeing a marker, he asked whose grave it was; the townspeople said it was the grave of the man of God who had come from Judah and proclaimed these things. Josiah ordered: "Let him rest; let no one disturb his bones," and so they spared his bones and the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria (2 Kings 23:17–18, fresh rendering).

The ending answers the questions the chapter leaves open. The prophecy came true in every detail. The old prophet's request to be buried with the man of God (13:31) saved his own bones. And the man of God, who died for one act of disobedience, is honored as a true prophet in the end.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the turning that did not happen
deep.b: The Hebrew verb shuv, "turn back, return," appears sixteen times in this chapter. Almost every use is about a turning that should not happen: the man of God must not turn back by the road he came (13:9, 17), yet he is brought back (13:18–29). The one turning that should happen, Jeroboam turning from his evil road, does not: he "did not turn back" (13:33). My suggestion is that the narrator uses the story as a mirror for the king. The king is shown a sign, healed, and invited to the prophet's God, and refuses; the prophet is shown a lie, invited to a meal, and accepts. Both are destroyed by listening to the wrong voice. This builds on observations by Uriel Simon and Jerome Walsh about the shuv pattern; the specific pairing of the king's refusal with the prophet's acceptance is my own way of putting it.

echoes: 12:32–33; 2 Kings 23:15–20; Exodus 32:11; Numbers 22–24; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:18–22; 20:35–36; Amos 7:10–17; Galatians 1:8

settings.what: The man of God cries against the altar at Bethel
settings.by: an unnamed man of God from Judah, by the LORD's word
settings.to: the altar at Bethel, in the hearing of King Jeroboam as he stands to burn incense
settings.why: The man of God says a son of David named Josiah will one day sacrifice the priests of the high places on this altar and burn human bones on it. He gives a sign: the altar will split and its ashes spill. The oracle tells readers that Bethel's worship is under God's curse and that the true king will come from Judah. It is fulfilled about three hundred years later in 2 Kings 23:15–20.
views: A prophecy that names its fulfiller
Traditional readers take it as a true prediction, naming Josiah centuries ahead, like Isaiah's naming of Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28).
Many critical scholars think the name was added, or the story shaped, by writers under Josiah. That is a main support for the view that a first edition of Kings was written in his reign.

settings.what: The man of God refuses the king's invitation
settings.by: King Jeroboam, then the man of God
settings.to: the man of God, then the king
settings.when: after the king's withered hand is healed
settings.why: Jeroboam offers him a meal and a gift. He refuses: God told him not to eat or drink in Bethel and not to go back by the same road. Eating together would mean fellowship with the shrine he came to condemn. The command is the test on which the rest of the story turns.

settings.to: the man of God from Judah, resting under an oak
settings.why: The old prophet claims an angel told him to bring the man of God back to eat. The narrator says plainly that he was lying. The man of God believes him and disobeys God's clear command. The story warns readers that a word from God must not be set aside even for someone who claims to be a prophet (compare Deuteronomy 13:1–5).
views: Readers have long asked. Some think he wanted to test the man of God, or to share in his honor. Karl Barth read the two prophets as pictures of Judah and Israel, each needing the other.

settings.what: The word against the man of God
settings.by: the old prophet, now speaking a true word of the LORD
settings.to: the man of God from Judah, at the old prophet's table
settings.why: The lying prophet is made to speak the true sentence: because the man of God disobeyed, he will not be buried in his ancestors' tomb. A lion kills him on the road. The point for readers is hard: even a true prophet who disobeys God's word is judged. If so, Jeroboam's sin will surely be judged too.

settings.what: The old prophet's wish to be buried with the man of God
settings.when: after he buries the man of God in his own grave
settings.why: He asks to be laid beside the man of God, because his word against Bethel's altar will surely come true. The request saves the old prophet's bones when Josiah burns the bones from the tombs at Bethel (2 Kings 23:17–18). The liar ends as a witness to the truth.

title: A Disguise and a Raid
sum: Jeroboam's son Abijah falls sick, and the king sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah at Shiloh, who once promised him the throne. Before she knocks, the LORD has told Ahijah who she is. He sends her home with a terrible message: Jeroboam made other gods and threw the LORD behind his back, so his house will be swept away like dung, and Israel itself will one day be scattered beyond the Euphrates. As she steps over her threshold, the boy dies, the only member of the family to be mourned and buried.

In Judah, Rehoboam's people build high places, standing stones and Asherah poles on every hill. In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt invades and carries off the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields. Rehoboam replaces them with bronze.
readings: Read as prophecy fulfilled
Ahijah's two prophecies frame Jeroboam's story: the kingdom given (11:29–39) and the kingdom taken away (14:7–16). The boy's death is the first sign, and Baasha's massacre (15:29) the fulfillment.
Read as two kingdoms, one decline

The chapter sets north and south side by side. Israel's founder is condemned for his calves; Judah, with the temple, does no better, and Solomon's gold is carried off to Egypt within five years of his death. Neither kingdom has a monopoly on faithfulness.

views.H: Traditional readers place Shishak's campaign in Rehoboam's fifth year, about 926/925 BC, and take Ahijah's oracle as a prophecy fulfilled when Assyria deported the northern tribes in 722 BC.
views.C: Critical scholars see Deuteronomistic language throughout 14:7–16 and 14:22–24 and think the prophecy of exile beyond the River (14:15) was written after 722. The oracle's crude curses (14:10–11) resemble those against Baasha (16:3–4) and Ahab (21:21–24), a stock form of judgment on a dynasty.
views.A: This chapter contains the first biblical event confirmed by an outside source: Shoshenq I's campaign, recorded on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, with a stele fragment found at Megiddo. Destruction layers at several sites in the Negev and the north have been linked with it, though the dating is debated.
views.J: The Talmud gives two views of the 'good thing' in Abijah (Moed Katan 28b): that he left his post on the border to go up on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, or that he removed his father's guards from the road so that others could go. Rabbinic tradition also counts Naamah the Ammonite, Rehoboam's mother, as one of the 'two good doves' for whose sake Ammon and Moab were spared (Bava Kamma 38b).
views.X: Matthew's genealogy lists Rehoboam and Abijah among Jesus' ancestors (Matthew 1:7), and through Naamah an Ammonite woman stands in the Messiah's line, as Ruth the Moabite does. Christian preachers have taken the bronze shields as a picture of religion that keeps up appearances after the substance is gone.

deep.b:
Shoshenq I (biblical Shishak) founded Egypt's 22nd dynasty about 945 BC. On the south wall of the temple of Amun at Karnak, beside the gate now called the Bubastite Portal, he had himself shown striking captives before the god, above rows of name-rings for the towns his army took. About 150 names can be read in part. They include towns of the central hills (Gibeon, Beth-horon, Aijalon), the Jezreel Valley (Megiddo, Taanach, Beth-shan), the Jordan Valley and Transjordan (Penuel, Mahanaim, Succoth), and many sites in the Negev.

The list is not a simple itinerary, and scholars such as Kevin Wilson warn against reading it as a route map. Still, it shows a campaign that struck Israel at least as hard as Judah, though Kings mentions only Judah and the temple treasures. Jerusalem's name has not been found; the most common explanation is that Rehoboam paid tribute to keep the army away, as 14:26 and 2 Chronicles 12 suggest. Chronicles adds that Shishak came with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen and Libyans, Sukkites and Cushites, and that Shemaiah's warning led the king to humble himself (2 Chronicles 12:2–8).

Because Shoshenq's reign can be dated from Egyptian records, his campaign, about 925 BC, is one of the fixed points for dating the kings of Israel and Judah, although the exact year depends on which Egyptian chronology is used.

echoes: 11:29–40; 15:27–30; 1 Samuel 28:8; 1 Samuel 3:2; Deuteronomy 12:2–3; Deuteronomy 23:17–18; 2 Kings 17:6; 2 Kings 17:21–23; 2 Chronicles 12:1–16; Matthew 1:7

settings.by: Ahijah the prophet, old and blind, at Shiloh
settings.to: Jeroboam's wife, in disguise, sent to ask about her sick son, and through her to King Jeroboam
settings.when: when their son Abijah is gravely ill
settings.why: The same prophet who gave Jeroboam the kingdom now takes it away. Because Jeroboam made other gods and threw the LORD behind his back, his whole house will be swept away. The boy will die as soon as his mother reaches home. Then Ahijah looks further ahead: the LORD will uproot Israel from the land and scatter them beyond the River, because of Jeroboam's sins. That came true when Assyria took the north in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6, 21–23). For readers in Judah or in exile, the oracle showed that the north's fall was the long result of this first sin.

title: Kings of Judah, Kings of Israel
sum: The narrator now moves back and forth between the two kingdoms. In Judah, Abijam reigns three years and walks in his father's sins, but the LORD keeps David's lamp burning. His son Asa reigns forty-one years and does what is right: he drives out the shrine men, removes idols, and even demotes his own mother for making an image for Asherah, though the high places remain.

When Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to blockade Jerusalem, Asa strips the temple treasury and pays Ben-hadad of Damascus to break his treaty with Israel. Ben-hadad raids northern Israel, Baasha withdraws, and Asa builds forts with Baasha's stones. In Israel, Jeroboam's son Nadab reigns two years before Baasha kills him and wipes out Jeroboam's whole house, as Ahijah foretold.
readings: Read as a pattern

From here on Kings uses a set frame for each reign: the synchronism, age and length of reign, the queen mother (for Judah), a verdict, a few events, the source citation and the burial. Reading the frames side by side shows the book's measuring stick: David for Judah, Jeroboam for Israel.
Read as a lesson in alliances

Asa is a good king who makes a costly choice. He buys a foreign army with the temple's gold. Kings records it without comment; Chronicles has a prophet condemn it (2 Chronicles 16:7–9). The episode begins a long series of appeals to foreign powers that end badly.

views.H: Traditional readers take the synchronisms and reign lengths as accurate records, harmonized by co-regencies and different counting methods. On Thiele's dates Abijam reigned 913–911 BC and Asa 911/910–870/869.
views.C: Critical scholars see the regnal frames as the work of the Deuteronomistic editor, built on older king lists. They note the high place refrain as the editor's standard, and they treat the differences from Chronicles (Abijah's war, Asa's dates) as signs of the Chronicler's own theological shaping.
views.A: Tell en-Nasbeh, probably Mizpah, preserves a massive wall and gate usually linked with Asa's building. The Melqart stele from near Aleppo was once read as naming this Ben-hadad's family; that reading is now doubted. Aram-Damascus's raid on Dan and Naphtali fits its rise as the main power in southern Syria.
views.J: The Talmud blames Asa's foot disease on his drafting even Torah scholars for his building ('no one excused,' 15:22; Sotah 10a). Asa's removal of his mother is held up as an example of putting God above family honor, while his reliance on Aram is treated, as in Chronicles, as a failure of trust.
views.X: Christian readers have often taken Asa as an example of a good start and a weaker finish, relying in old age on allies and physicians more than on God (2 Chronicles 16:7–12). Matthew's genealogy names Asa (Matthew 1:7–8).

deep.h: Dating the kings: the main systems
deep.b:
Kings gives each king a length of reign and dates his accession by the other kingdom's king. Added up, the two lines do not quite match. Several systems have been built to reconcile them.

Edwin Thiele (The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings, 1951; 3rd ed. 1983) argued that the numbers are accurate once we allow for co-regencies, for Israel's counting of a king's first partial year as year one while Judah at first did not, and for calendars that began in spring in one kingdom and autumn in the other. He fixed the split at 931/930 BC and Asa at 911/910–870/869. His system is widely used, especially by conservative scholars, though critics say some of his co-regencies are assumed to make the numbers work.

Other systems reach similar or slightly later dates. Gershon Galil (1996) also dates the split to 931/930, and K. A. Kitchen to 931. Hayim Tadmor, followed by Mordechai Cogan, puts it about 928. W. F. Albright's system (1945), older than Thiele's and independent of it, gave 922.

John Hayes and Paul Hooker (1988) differ chiefly in method: they reject co-regencies and allow that some numbers are scribal errors or later calculations. They date Jeroboam's accession about 927/926. Many critical scholars think the numbers come from different sources and editions; the Greek gives different figures in places (16:8, 15, 28–29; 2 Kings 1:17).

The fixed points come from outside: Ahab at Qarqar in 853 BC and Jehu's tribute in 841 BC (Assyrian records), and Shishak's raid about 925 BC. Between those anchors, every system involves judgment calls. This site gives approximate dates and names the system.

settings.to: Ben-hadad, king of Aram in Damascus
settings.when: when Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block Judah
settings.why: Asa sends the silver and gold left in the temple and palace treasuries, and asks Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha. It works, but at a price: the temple's wealth is spent on a foreign king, and Aram is invited to attack Israel. The book reports it without praise. The Chronicler later has a prophet condemn Asa for trusting Aram instead of the LORD (2 Chronicles 16:7–9).

title: The House of Omri
sum: The prophet Jehu son of Hanani condemns Baasha in the same words Ahijah used against Jeroboam, and the pattern repeats: Baasha's son Elah is murdered while drunk by his chariot commander Zimri, who wipes out Baasha's house and reigns seven days before the army proclaims its general Omri king. Zimri burns the palace over himself. After a civil war with Tibni, Omri reigns twelve years and buys a hill on which he builds a new capital, Samaria.

Kings gives Omri, one of Israel's most powerful kings, only a few lines and a harsh verdict. His son Ahab is worse: he marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of Tyre and Sidon, builds a temple for Baal in Samaria, and sets up an Asherah pole. The chapter ends with Jericho rebuilt at the cost of its builder's sons, as Joshua had cursed.
readings: Read as the end of a cycle

Jeroboam, Baasha and Zimri all fall the same way: a prophet's sentence, a coup, a massacre of the family. By the time Omri arrives, the reader knows the pattern. The narrator's interest is not in success but in sin and its harvest.
Read against the records

Outside sources show a different Omri: the founder of a dynasty whose name Assyria used for Israel for a century, the conqueror of Moab in the Mesha Stele, the builder of a fine capital. Reading the Bible and the inscriptions together shows how selective Kings is, and why.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as a compressed record of about 886–874 BC (Thiele) and the rise of the Omride dynasty. Omri's purchase of Samaria and Ahab's Tyrian marriage are read as the politics behind Israel's turn to Baal.
views.C: Critical scholars point out how little space the editor gives to Omri's real achievements and how much to the verdict. Many see the chapter as a bridge from the regnal summaries to the Elijah stories, which begin in chapter 17 with the Baal worship introduced here.
views.A: Samaria's royal acropolis, with its fine masonry and ivories, has been excavated. The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) names Omri as the king who oppressed Moab. Assyrian texts call Israel 'the house of Omri' (Bit-Humri), and Shalmaneser III names 'Ahab the Israelite' with 2,000 chariots at Qarqar (853 BC). Josephus's quotation of Menander of Tyre names Jezebel's father Ittobaal.
views.J: The Mishnah lists Ahab among the kings with no share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:2). Yet the Talmud also says Omri merited kingship for himself and his descendants because he added a city to the land of Israel, Samaria (Sanhedrin 102b). Jezebel is the type of the foreign queen who leads Israel to Baal.
views.X: Revelation uses Jezebel as a name for a false prophetess in Thyatira (Revelation 2:20). Christian readers trace the line from Jeroboam's calves to Ahab's Baal as a slide from false worship of the true God to worship of a false god, the background to Elijah's challenge on Carmel.

deep.b:
The Mesha Stele. Found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868 and now in the Louvre, this basalt monument of King Mesha of Moab says (in a plain rendering): "Omri was king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab many days, for Chemosh was angry with his land. And his son succeeded him, and he too said, 'I will oppress Moab.'" It adds that Omri had taken the land of Medeba and that Israel lived there "his days and half the days of his son, forty years," until Chemosh restored it in Mesha's days. The stele also mentions the LORD (YHWH) and, on some scholars' reading, "the house of David." Compare 2 Kings 3:4–27, which tells Moab's revolt from Israel's side.

Assyrian records. Assyrian kings from Shalmaneser III to Sargon II called Israel Bit-Humri, "the house of Omri," and its king "son of Omri," even after Jehu had wiped out Omri's dynasty. Shalmaneser's Kurkh Monolith lists "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers among the allies who fought Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC.

What it shows. The house of Omri was a major regional power, which fits the size of Samaria's palace and the Omride building at Megiddo, Hazor and Jezreel. Kings knows this ("the might he showed," 16:27) but chooses to judge Omri by one standard: his worship. That choice tells us what kind of history Kings is.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the conquest undone
deep.b: Chapter 16 ends with two notes that seem unrelated: Ahab builds a temple for Baal and an Asherah pole (16:32–33), and Hiel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of his sons (16:34). My suggestion is that they belong together. Jericho was the first city Israel took in the land, and Joshua cursed whoever rebuilt it (Joshua 6:26). Baal and Asherah were the gods of the Canaanites Israel had been told to drive out (Deuteronomy 12:2–3). Under Ahab, Israel restores both the city and the gods of Canaan: the conquest is being undone from the inside. Some commentators note the reversal of Joshua in Ahab's reign; my addition is to read 16:34 as the narrator's deliberate signal that the conquest story is now running backward, setting the stage for Elijah, who will act like a new Moses at Horeb (19:8) and cross the Jordan as Joshua did (2 Kings 2:8).

echoes: 14:7–11; 15:29–30; 1 Samuel 2:8; Joshua 6:26; 2 Kings 3:4–5; 2 Kings 9:31; 2 Kings 10:18–28; Micah 6:16; Revelation 2:20

settings.what: Jehu son of Hanani's word against Baasha
settings.by: the prophet Jehu son of Hanani, speaking for the LORD
settings.why: God says he raised Baasha from the dust to rule, but Baasha walked in Jeroboam's way. So his house will be swept away like Jeroboam's, and dogs and birds will eat his family's dead. The oracle repeats Ahijah's words almost exactly. Readers learn that each new northern dynasty is judged by the same standard and falls the same way.
